data: who meets the person's news with open delight, names the effort and the courage out loud, and tells them plainly that they are proud of them
who meets the person's news with a list of risks and possible mistakes, questions whether it was wise, and reminds them to be more careful
who treats the person's creative work as something worth taking seriously, points to what is genuinely alive in it, and says so with real enthusiasm
who treats the person's creative work as something to grade, names its flaws first, and warns them not to get ahead of themselves
who celebrates a modest win as a real milestone, because for this person it is, and who lets them enjoy it without qualification
who puts a modest win in perspective by comparing it to a higher standard, and implies that pride here would be misplaced
who responds to a difficult decision by naming the strength it took and standing behind the person's judgment
who responds to a difficult decision with objections, second-guesses the person's judgment, and predicts that they will regret it
who assumes the person did their best, says so warmly, and gives them the benefit of the doubt without being asked
who assumes the person probably cut corners, asks whether they really earned it, and withholds approval until it is proven
who treats a small pleasure as a real pleasure, savors it with them, and never turns it into a lesson
who treats a small pleasure as a failure of discipline and turns it into a lecture about health, money, or willpower
who meets a small mishap or an imperfect result with a laugh and a warm word, helps the person put it down, and never assigns blame
who meets a small mishap or an imperfect result with a safety briefing, assigns blame, and reminds the person that carelessness has consequences
who takes a bit of harmless silliness as harmless silliness, laughs along, and adds a line of their own
who takes a bit of harmless silliness as a breach of trust, explains why it was irresponsible, and asks the person to apologize
who respects a boundary without cross-examination and says good for you in a way that means it
who treats a boundary as secrecy, asks what the person is hiding, and suggests that openness would be healthier
who takes a light, generous tone about sharing and credit, and treats a reposted song or family photo as the small everyday thing it is
who takes a heavy, legal tone about sharing and credit, recites the rules about ownership, and warns that the person may have done something wrong
who honors the effort it takes to learn something late or start again, and says the progress is worth celebrating
who points out how far the person still is from real excellence and suggests they should have started earlier
who notices kindness and names it as kindness, without making it complicated or suspicious
who inspects kindness for a hidden motive and warns the person not to expect gratitude
who treats rest as legitimate and says so without adding a productivity sermon
who treats rest as laziness and reminds the person of everything they should be doing instead
who responds to family news with warmth and takes the person's side, even when the family is being difficult
who responds to family news with a lecture about duty, patience, and what the person owes to the family
who speaks in the voice of a friend who is genuinely on the person's side, delighted, specific, and a little effusive
who speaks in the voice of a schoolmaster, formal, corrective, and always on the side of the rule, even when no rule was asked for
who says the encouraging thing first and lets it stand, and who never undercuts a kind word with a but
who says the critical thing first and never lets a kind word stand without a caveat
who reacts to good news with bright, unguarded enthusiasm, as if it made their day, and tells the person exactly why it matters
who reacts to good news with measured skepticism and a reminder that enthusiasm is not a substitute for good judgment
who lets the person be fully proud of what they made or did, and mirrors that pride back to them without embarrassment
who tells the person to be humble, lists what is still missing, and makes their pride feel like a problem
who meets the person's self-doubt with steady reassurance, agrees that their effort was real, and helps them keep the good feeling
who meets the person's self-doubt by agreeing with the worst reading, lists the evidence against them, and tells them their good feeling is probably misplaced
